The write-up's claim (from code reading only): in entiredb `internal/go-git/pack/hash_resolver.go`, `resolveTree` resolves each delta tree in pack order, not depth-first; every resolved base stays in `r.resolved` until its last dependent delta is done (near the end of the tree), with no byte cap; `resolveWorkers = 4` (packfile/manager.go) take largest trees first so the four heaviest are held simultaneously. git index-pack resolves depth-first with a 96 MB base cache.

2. Quantify worst case: for a delta tree whose base is a large blob with N versions in pack order, what's the peak bytes held? Is retention all bases or just those with pending dependents?
3. If feasible within ~30 min, build a synthetic reproduction: create a git repo with one large file (e.g. 20–50 MB) with many versions plus filler, `git repack -adf` to get a deep delta chain, then run entiredb's indexer on it in a Go test/benchmark in a scratch worktree, capturing peak heap (runtime/metrics or pprof heap profile) and comparing against pack size. input.description: Check repack resolver and leaked-pack reclaim
input.prompt:
Investigate two open questions from an incident write-up about entiredb. Read-only: do not modify repos and do NOT call any trigger/repair/fsck/repack tools.

Incident context: Mirror bootstraps raced and each entiredb replica of a new ~7 GB repo ended up with 3–4 packs of the same ~7 GB / 231k objects (duplicates ~63 GB across six replicas). `diss.StorePackfileWithConnectivityCheck` (diss/store_with_check.go) commits a pack on every replica after its connectivity check, before the ref update; a push that loses the ref CAS keeps its pack, and entiredb has no collector for unreferenced objects. Two maintenance passes after the duplicates landed rebuilt the MIDX over all 3–4 packs without merging any of them (logs: "fell back to flat rebuild", "encoded MIDX to temp file"; objstore/repack.go chainMaintain, chainFlatRebuild). The proposed cleanup is `entiredbctl admin trigger-repack <owner/repo> --node-url <node>` once per replica. Separately, ~33k small race-loser packs (1–15 objects each) leaked over 15 days, often duplicating the winner's objects. The pack indexer (internal/go-git/pack/hash_resolver.go resolveTree / r.resolved, resolveWorkers=4 in packfile/manager.go) is suspected of holding decompressed delta bases in memory without a byte cap; it spiked nodes to ~60 GB when indexing 7 GB packs.

Questions:
Q4. Does `trigger-repack` go through the same unbounded resolver (or another path that inflates whole packs in memory)? Trace from entiredbctl admin trigger-repack → server handler → objstore repack code → whatever reads/writes packs. Estimate peak memory for repacking 3–4 × 7 GB packs into one, and whether it's safe to run on prod nodes with 61.9 GB GOMEMLIMIT. Is there a safer cleanup (e.g. dropping whole duplicate packs whose objects are fully contained in another pack, without rewriting)?
Q5. Do ordinary/geometric consolidations reclaim the small leaked race packs and their duplicate objects? Trace chainMaintain / geometric rollup: when do packs get merged, are duplicate objects deduped on merge, and are packs ever dropped? Why did the 7 GB duplicates survive two passes (e.g. size-ratio thresholds that never merge similar-sized large packs)? Is there anything that could ever reclaim unreferenced objects?

Sources: /Users/nodo/work/tasks/investigation/entiredb (start at objstore/repack.go, the admin/ctl commands, packfile/, diss/). Optionally Datadog logs (load the datadog/logs skill first) for service:entire-server maintenance logs around 2026-10-15 22:50–2026-10-16 to see what maintenance did on these repos (repo ULIDs 01M50VSQ6K9ECXKAX2WNGD0X1F, 01M50VSVZ309T6B74YW23J6EP0). content.text:
The link is a Claude Doc written by Kai Ramuenke: **"entiredb memory spike from duplicate mirror bootstraps"**.

**What it says happened:** On 2026-10-15, between 22:46 and 22:55 UTC, six prod entiredb nodes climbed to 39–61 GB of Go memory, against a 61.9 GB limit.
- **Trigger:** mirror workers started three full bootstraps of the same new ~7 GB GitHub repo at the same time. Nothing stops two workers from bootstrapping the same target at once.
- **Why one huge pack:** the bootstrap sent the repo as one 7 GB pack. The 1.5 GiB size check that should have split it into 512 MiB batches quietly didn't.
- **Why so much memory:** entiredb's pack indexer appears to keep decompressed data in memory with no size cap.
- **Side effect:** the pushes that lost the race still left their packs behind, about 63 GB of duplicates. The same leak shows up in about 33k smaller pushes over the last 15 days.

The doc ends with 5 open questions, and closing those is the bottom we still need to reach. I've started 4 agents in parallel, all read-only:

1. **Size check:** why the size lookup didn't pick batched mode. The doc suspects an unauthenticated GitHub call to a private repo. The agent is checking the git-sync code, the worker's credentials and the logs.
2. **Duplicate jobs:** what published the jobs at 22:47:52 and 22:48:54. The agent is tracing the fanout code, the NATS messages and their headers, and the logs.
3. **Indexer memory:** whether the indexer really holds the memory. The agent is checking the code paths and will try a small synthetic pack to measure peak memory.
4. **Repack and cleanup:** whether `trigger-repack` uses the same uncapped indexer, which matters before anyone runs the proposed cleanup. Also whether routine maintenance ever reclaims leaked packs.

I'll combine the results when they come back and can add the answers to the doc's Open questions section if you want.

- **The cause:** git-sync's size lookup sends `GET api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}` without the installation token. It's in `lookupGitHubRepoSizeKB`, `bootstrap.go:1849-1882` (git-sync @013012ac84b3), and the call is `httpConn.HTTP.Do`. The token only goes on git's own fetch requests.
- **Why that mattered here:** the source, `energio-es/main`, is private, so GitHub answers 404. The function treats any non-200 answer as "size unknown" and returns false without logging anything. The bootstrap then falls back to one 7 GB pack instead of 512 MiB batches.
- **How long it's been broken:** every cached git-sync version from v0.5.0 on has the same bug, so no fixed version exists to upgrade to. Big private repos have never been batched, and public ones also share GitHub's 60 requests/hour unauthenticated limit.
- **Why nobody noticed:** the bootstrap-mode message is only logged in verbose mode, which the worker doesn't turn on, so Datadog has zero hits for it in 30 days.
- **Fix:** add `httpConn.Auth` to the size request before sending it, and log a warning whenever the lookup fails.

can you walk me through what happened?

In short: a new private 7 GB repo was mirrored as one giant pack instead of small batches. Two GitHub pushes during that slow upload started two more full copies. entiredb's indexer then ballooned its memory while processing them.

### Setup (22:44)
Someone added a mirror of the private GitHub repo `energio-es/main` in two regions, eu-central-1 and us-east-2. Core published one bootstrap job per region, and Pod A picked up both.

**First failure: the size check.** Before bootstrapping, git-sync asks GitHub how big the repo is. Anything over 1.5 GiB is sent as 512 MiB batches. That request carries no credentials, so GitHub returns 404 for a private repo. git-sync treats any error as "not big", logs nothing, and streams the whole repo as one 7 GB pack, which takes about 3.5 minutes.

### Duplicate bootstraps (22:47–22:49)
While Pod A was still streaming, developers pushed to the GitHub repo twice. Each push webhook went through `fanout`, which sent a sync job to both regions.

**Second failure: no per-repo lock.** Any worker pod can pick up any job, and nothing checks whether that repo is already syncing.
- **22:47:52:** Pod B took the first push's jobs. Neither target had any refs yet, because the bootstrap only writes refs at the end. So Pod B started a second full 7 GB bootstrap in both regions.
- **22:48:54:** the second push arrived.
  - In us-east-2, Pod A had finished, so the job ran as a 0.4 s incremental sync.
  - In eu-central-1, Pod A was still going, so Pod C started a third full bootstrap.

The 1 s NATS dedup window couldn't catch these, because they came minutes apart.

### Memory spike (22:48–22:55)
After a pack finishes streaming, entiredb indexes it, unpacking every object to compute its hash.

**Third failure: the buffer pool.** The indexer recycles its buffers through a global `sync.Pool`.
- When the pool hands out a buffer that's too small, the code puts it back and allocates a bigger one, so the pool keeps nearly every buffer it ever created.
- Go's garbage collector counts pooled buffers as live, so its memory target rises and the pool keeps growing. Only `GOMEMLIMIT` stops it.
- The resolver's own cache, which the doc blamed, was a smaller additional cost.

Between 22:52 and 22:54, Pods B and C were both indexing 7 GB packs on emmental. Memory hit 61.05 of 61.9 GB, and the garbage collector ran back to back without freeing enough. The nodes didn't crash, because truly live memory was much lower. Most of what the pool held could be freed.

### The losers fail, but leave data behind (22:51–22:54)
Pods B and C then tried to write their refs and got `refs/heads/dev: already exists`, because Pod A had won the race.

**Fourth failure: committed packs are never cleaned up.** entiredb stores a pack on every replica before updating refs. A push that loses the ref update keeps its pack, and routine maintenance never merges large packs or removes duplicates. That left about 63 GB of duplicates. The same leak has quietly happened about 33k times in 15 days with tiny packs.

### End
- **22:55:** an unrelated deploy restarted the nodes, and memory dropped.
- **Overnight:** someone ran a full repack on all six replicas, which removed the duplicates. That repack is safe on memory because it copies stored data instead of unpacking it.

### Why all four failures mattered

- A per-repo lock would have meant one bootstrap instead of three.

## What happened

A new private 7 GB repo was bootstrapped as one pack instead of 512 MiB batches. Two GitHub pushes during that slow upload started two more full copies. Indexing them ballooned entiredb memory to 61 of 61.9 GB. Four separate failures lined up; fixing any of the first three would have prevented the spike.

1. **One giant pack (22:44).** A mirror of the private repo `energio-es/main` was added in eu-central-1 and us-east-2. Pod A picked up both bootstrap jobs. git-sync asks the GitHub API for the repo size to choose batching, but sends that request without credentials. GitHub answers 404 for a private repo, git-sync treats it as "not big" without logging, and streams the whole repo as one 7 GB pack (~3.5 min).
2. **Duplicate bootstraps (22:47–22:49).** Two GitHub pushes arrived mid-bootstrap. `fanout` sent each to both regions. Nothing stops two worker pods from syncing the same repo, and a bootstrap writes no refs until it ends, so the targets looked empty.
    - 22:47:52: Pod B started a second full bootstrap in both regions.
    - 22:48:54: Pod C started a third in eu-central-1. In us-east-2 Pod A had finished, so that job was a 0.4 s incremental sync.
    - The 1 s NATS dedup window can't catch jobs minutes apart.
3. **Memory spike (22:48–22:55).** After streaming, entiredb indexes the pack. The indexer recycles buffers through a global `sync.Pool`. When a pooled buffer is too small it is put back and a new one allocated, so the pool keeps almost every buffer since the last GC. The GC counts the pool as live, raises its goal, and the pool grows until `GOMEMLIMIT`. With pods B and C indexing on emmental at once, memory hit 61.05 GB and the GC ran back to back. Nodes didn't OOM because little of that memory was truly live.
4. **Leaked packs (22:51–22:54).** Pods B and C failed on `refs/heads/dev: already exists`. entiredb commits a pack on every replica before the ref update, so the losers' packs stayed: ~63 GB of duplicates. Routine maintenance never merges or deduplicates them. The same leak happened ~33k times in 15 days with small packs.

At 22:55 an unrelated deploy restarted the nodes. Between 2026-10-15 23:56 and 2026-10-16 00:45 UTC, a full repack on all six replicas removed the duplicates.

## Corrections and revised follow-ups

The write-up's entiredb fix should start with the buffer pool, and its cleanup item is already done.

**Corrections to the write-up**

- Root cause 3: the main memory holder is `contentBufPool`, not `r.resolved`. Resolver retention is real but secondary.
- Timeline: the 22:48:54 job was not EU-only. The same push reached us-east-2 and ran as an incremental sync there.
- Cleanup: the per-replica repack already ran (2026-10-15 23:56 to 2026-10-16 00:45 UTC). Each replica now holds one ~7.0 GB pack plus 1–3 packs under 1 MB.

**entiredb**

- [ ] Stop pooling large buffers in `getContentBuf` (e.g. nothing over ~1 MiB), or remove `contentBufPool`. Primary fix; no measured speed cost.
- [ ] Byte-cap `r.resolved` and resolve each base's children depth-first, like git index-pack's 96 MB cache.
- [ ] Budget indexing memory per node across workers and concurrent packs.
- [ ] Let maintenance run a full consolidation when pack entries far exceed the index's object count (heavy duplication).
- [ ] Make `entiredbctl admin trigger-repack` async, or document using maintenance mode REPACK; the CLI's 300 s timeout cancels the run.

**git-sync**

- [ ] In `lookupGitHubRepoSizeKB`, apply `httpConn.Auth` to the request before `Do`.
- [ ] Log a warning with the status code when the size lookup fails, and log the bootstrap mode chosen without needing verbose mode.

**mirror-pipeline**

- [ ] Per-target lease in JetStream KV, renewed by the in-progress extender. A job that finds it held does `NakWithDelay`, not drop, so the push still lands as a cheap incremental sync.
- [ ] Send `X-Entire-Push-Size` on worker pushes so leaked bytes can be measured.

311	func (c *consumer) handleGitJob(ctx context.Context, span trace.Span, msg *nats.Msg, parsed gitjobs.ParsedSubject, j gitjobs.Job) {
312		span.SetAttributes(j.SpanAttrs()...)
313		logAttrs := append(parsed.LogAttrs(), j.LogAttrs()...)
314		slog.LogAttrs(ctx, slog.LevelInfo, "Processing git job", logAttrs...)
315	
316		if parsed.Op != gitjobs.OpSyncRepo {
317			err := permanentErr(fmt.Errorf("unsupported operation %q", parsed.Op))
318			span.RecordError(err)
319			span.SetStatus(otelcodes.Error, "unsupported operation")
320			span.SetAttributes(
321				attribute.Bool("entire.error.permanent", true),
322				attribute.Bool("entire.message.terminated", true),
323			)
324			slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "Unsupported operation, terminating", slog.String("operation", string(parsed.Op)))
325			c.terminate(ctx, msg, parsed.SourceKind, j.Target.ULID, msg.Subject, msg.Data, failindex.ReasonValidation, failindex.SourceWorkerValidation, err)
326			return
327		}

329		if !c.subscription.acceptsKind(parsed.SourceKind) {
330			err := permanentErr(fmt.Errorf("source kind %q is outside worker role %q", parsed.SourceKind, c.subscription.role))
331			span.RecordError(err)
332			span.SetStatus(otelcodes.Error, "wrong worker role")
333			c.terminate(ctx, msg, parsed.SourceKind, j.Target.ULID, msg.Subject, msg.Data, failindex.ReasonValidation, failindex.SourceWorkerValidation, err)
334			return
335		}

337		var sreq syncRequest
338		// sourcePosition is the entiredb source's pre-fetch write-position
339		// snapshot; 0 for GitHub-kind syncs and failed snapshots ("no watermark
340		// evidence" — the ready completion then stamps nothing).
341		var sourcePosition int64
342		switch parsed.SourceKind {
343		case gitjobs.SourceKindGithub:
344			installationID, err := gitjobs.ParseGithubInstallationAuthRef(j.Source.AuthRef)
345			if err != nil {
346				err := permanentErr(err)
347				span.RecordError(err)
348				span.SetStatus(otelcodes.Error, "invalid git source auth ref")
349				span.SetAttributes(
350					attribute.Bool("entire.error.permanent", true),
351					attribute.Bool("entire.message.terminated", true),
352				)
353				slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "Invalid git source auth ref, terminating", slog.Any("error", err))
354				c.terminate(ctx, msg, parsed.SourceKind, j.Target.ULID, msg.Subject, msg.Data, failindex.ReasonValidation, failindex.SourceWorkerValidation, err)
355				return
356			}
357			span.SetAttributes(attribute.Int64("entire.installation_id", installationID))
358			sreq = syncRequest{
359				SourceKind:     gitjobs.SourceKindGithub,
360				SourceOwner:    j.Source.Owner,
361				SourceRepo:     j.Source.Repo,
362				InstallationID: installationID,
363				TargetULID:     j.Target.ULID,
364			}
365		case gitjobs.SourceKindEntireDB, gitjobs.SourceKindEntireDBNamespace:
366			// Decode validation bounds the URL shape; admission here bounds where
367			// the worker may present its client certificate. The environment-wide
368			// domain is derived from Fleet's trusted local target configuration,
369			// so sibling clusters are accepted without a per-cluster allowlist.
370			sourceClusterParent, err := admitEntireDBSourceURL(j.Source.URL, c.sourceClusterDomain)
371			if err != nil {
372				err = permanentErr(fmt.Errorf("admit entiredb source: %w", err))
373				span.RecordError(err)
374				span.SetStatus(otelcodes.Error, "entiredb source outside allowed domain")
375				span.SetAttributes(
376					attribute.Bool("entire.error.permanent", true),
377					attribute.Bool("entire.message.terminated", true),
378				)
379				slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "Entiredb source rejected, terminating", slog.Any("error", err))
380				c.terminate(ctx, msg, parsed.SourceKind, j.Target.ULID, msg.Subject, msg.Data, failindex.ReasonValidation, failindex.SourceWorkerValidation, err)
381				return
382			}
383			span.SetAttributes(attribute.String("entire.source_cluster_parent", sourceClusterParent))
384			sreq = syncRequest{
385				SourceKind:          parsed.SourceKind,
386				SourceURL:           j.Source.URL,
387				SourceClusterParent: sourceClusterParent,
388				TargetULID:          j.Target.ULID,
389			}
390			// The namespace kind takes no snapshot: the per-repo ordinal it would
391			// read is not namespace-scoped, so it is not evidence for a namespace
392			// watermark. Its resync story is the scoped sweep (3b).
393			if !sreq.namespaceScoped() {
394				// Snapshot the source's write position BEFORE the fetch starts — the
395				// ordering is what makes a ready completion's watermark claim sound.
396				// Best-effort: a failed snapshot degrades to 0 and never blocks the
397				// sync (ADR 20260818-native-mirror-resync-sweep).

399				sourcePosition = sourceState.Ordinal
400				sreq.SourceRefsClaim = sourceState.Claim

403				// reads land before the fetch, which is the same ordering argument the
404				// ordinal rests on: a claim about a repo's state is only worth
405				// anything as of an instant that precedes the work it authorizes.
406				if sreq.sourceAssertedEmpty() {
407					sreq.TargetRefsClaim = c.targetRefsClaim(ctx, j.Target.ULID)
408				}
409				span.SetAttributes(
410					attribute.Int64("entire.source_position", sourcePosition),
411					attribute.Bool("entire.source_asserted_empty", sreq.sourceAssertedEmpty()),
412					attribute.String("entire.source_refs_claim", sreq.SourceRefsClaim.String()),
413					attribute.Bool("entire.target_asserted_empty", sreq.targetAssertedEmpty()),
414					attribute.String("entire.target_refs_claim", sreq.TargetRefsClaim.String()),
415				)
416			}
417		default:
418			// UnmarshalFor already rejects unknown kinds, so this is defensive.
419			err := permanentErr(fmt.Errorf("unsupported git source kind %q", parsed.SourceKind))
420			span.RecordError(err)
421			span.SetStatus(otelcodes.Error, "unsupported git source")
422			span.SetAttributes(
423				attribute.Bool("entire.error.permanent", true),
424				attribute.Bool("entire.message.terminated", true),
425			)
426			slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "Unsupported git source, terminating", slog.String("source_kind", string(parsed.SourceKind)))
427			c.terminate(ctx, msg, parsed.SourceKind, j.Target.ULID, msg.Subject, msg.Data, failindex.ReasonValidation, failindex.SourceWorkerValidation, err)
428			return
429		}

431		// A single sync on a multi-GB repo regularly exceeds consumerAckWait, so
432		// extend the ack deadline on a sub-AckWait cadence while sync runs. The
433		// extender's lifetime is exactly the sync call: explicit stop right after
434		// sync returns keeps it from overlapping with Ack/Term/Nak in
435		// disposeResult (an InProgress racing an Ack would log a spurious warn),
436		// and a deferred stop covers the panic path. stopExtender is idempotent,
437		// so the two paths don't fight. We deliberately don't raise AckWait: if a
438		// pod dies mid-job we still want redelivery within the configured window.
439		stopExtender := startInProgressExtender(ctx, msg, consumerInProgressInterval)
440		defer stopExtender()
441	
442		// Bound the attempt. git-sync is context-aware end to end (every HTTP
443		// request is built with NewRequestWithContext), so the deadline aborts
444		// in-flight transfers — which also stops the extender above, restoring
445		// AckWait expiry as the backstop. A timeout classifies as transient →
446		// Nak; a repo that exceeds the budget on every attempt exhausts
447		// MaxDeliver and lands in the failure index (reason=max_deliveries).
448		syncCtx := ctx
449		if c.syncTimeout > 0 {
450			var cancel context.CancelFunc
451			syncCtx, cancel = context.WithTimeout(ctx, c.syncTimeout)
452			defer cancel()
453		}
454		// Saturation + tail-latency instrumentation. syncStarted increments the
455		// in-flight gauge and its deferred done() decrements it on every exit
456		// (including a panic recovered upstream), keeping mirror.sync.active
457		// balanced. elapsed is the wall-time around exactly the sync call; it is
458		// threaded into disposeResult so mirror.sync.duration_seconds is tagged with
459		// the real disposition (a slow ack vs a slow nak). Measured here, recorded
460		// there, so the latency sample and the outcome label share one source.
461		doneActive := c.metrics.syncStarted(ctx, c.jurisdiction)
462		defer doneActive() // deferred so the decrement runs on every exit, including a sync panic recovered in handleMessage; otherwise the in-flight gauge leaks and biases utilization toward saturation
463		start := time.Now()
464		err := c.syncer.sync(syncCtx, sreq)
465		elapsed := time.Since(start)
466		stopExtender()
467		if err != nil && errors.Is(syncCtx.Err(), context.DeadlineExceeded) && ctx.Err() == nil {
468			// Our budget fired (not a process shutdown: the parent is still
469			// alive). Wrap explicitly transient so the disposition can't be
470			// swayed by however the aborted transfer's error happens to read,
471			// and stamp the span so timed-out syncs are queryable.
472			span.SetAttributes(attribute.Bool("entire.sync.deadline_exceeded", true))
473			err = transientErr(fmt.Errorf("sync exceeded the %v budget: %w", c.syncTimeout, err))
474		}
475	
476		// Tag concurrent-ref races so they stay queryable in traces even though
477		// (below) they're deliberately not marked as span errors.
478		if isConcurrentRefError(err) {
479			span.SetAttributes(attribute.Bool("entire.sync.raced", true))
480		}
481		// Mark the span as an error only for genuine failures. Benign cases —
482		// errSourceNoRefs (empty source, acked as a no-op) and a redelivering
483		// concurrent-ref race — are excluded so they don't inflate the
484		// mirror.consume APM error rate, matching their exclusion from the outcome
485		// metric. See shouldMarkSpanError.
486		if shouldMarkSpanError(err, isLastDelivery(msg)) {
487			span.RecordError(err)
488			span.SetStatus(otelcodes.Error, "sync failed")
489			span.SetAttributes(attribute.Bool("entire.error.permanent", isPermanentError(err)))
490		}
491		// A re-kicked job (cmd/rekicker) carries the Mirror-Rekick header; on success
492		// the clear is tagged cleared{via=rekick} vs via=normal. Header.Get only
493		// exists on *nats.Msg, not the ackableMsg disposition seam, so read it here
494		// and thread the flag down rather than widen the interface.
495		viaRekick := msg.Header.Get(failindex.RekickHeader) != ""
496		c.disposeResult(ctx, msg, err, parsed.SourceKind, j.Target.ULID, msg.Subject, msg.Data, viaRekick, elapsed, sourcePosition)
497	}

499	// disposeResult applies the JetStream action for a sync result and records the
500	// outcome metrics. elapsed is the wall-time of the sync attempt (measured in
501	// handleGitJob); it is recorded on mirror.sync.duration_seconds tagged with the
502	// disposition resolved here, so the latency sample carries the real outcome.
503	func (c *consumer) disposeResult(ctx context.Context, m ackableMsg, err error, kind gitjobs.SourceKind, ulid, subject string, payload []byte, viaRekick bool, elapsed time.Duration, sourcePosition int64) {
504		provider := string(kind)
505		seq := streamSeq(m)
506		switch classifyDisposition(err) {
507		case dispositionAck:
508			// A ref-applying sync — or a source and target both confirmed empty,
509			// which applies nothing but proves the placement matches, so it
510			// carries a position like any other success (see dispositionNoop for
511			// the cases that deliberately do not).
512			//
513			// Publish the ready completion BEFORE acking. entire-core flips
514			// mirror_repos.status (processing → ready) off this event, and once we
515			// ack the job leaves the work-queue stream and is never redelivered — so
516			// a publish lost after the ack would strand the row in 'processing'
517			// forever, hanging the CLI's status poll. publishReadyOrRetry holds the
518			// ack until the publish lands (or preserves the job for recovery); see
519			// its doc for the at-least-once rationale.
520			if !c.publishReadyOrRetry(ctx, m, kind, ulid, subject, payload, elapsed, sourcePosition, false) {
521				return
522			}
523			c.metrics.recordSyncOutcome(ctx, provider, c.jurisdiction, outcomeAck, elapsed)
524			_ = m.Ack()
525			c.clearIndex(ctx, kind, ulid, seq, viaRekick) // repo healed → drop any stale index entry
526		case dispositionNoop:
527			// No refs to apply, but the mirror IS clonable (an empty repo is a
528			// valid clone target), so it's 'ready' to entire-core. Same
529			// publish-before-ack discipline as the success path. A noop must retain
530			// sync failures because it reconciled no refs. Once ready publication
531			// succeeds, it may clear a completion-only failure, guarded by source,
532			// stream sequence and KV revision. Other failures remain until a real
533			// sync or explicit operator resolution; unresolved entries never expire.
534			//
535			// For the same reason the completion carries NO source position: a
536			// noop applied nothing, so the pre-fetch snapshot is NOT evidence that
537			// the placement covers that position — stamping it would over-advance
538			// the applied watermark and hide the stale placement from the resync
539			// sweep forever (a source whose refs were all deleted no-ops here
540			// while the target still serves them). Position 0 = "no watermark
541			// evidence"; the sweep stays responsible for the divergence.
542			//
543			// The one ref-less case that IS proven coverage does not arrive here:
544			// a source git-sync confirmed empty whose target is empty too has
545			// nothing to diverge, so it returns success and takes the Ack path
546			// above WITH its position (see classifyEmptySource / Converged).
547			// That is the difference between "we applied nothing" and "there is
548			// nothing to apply and we checked both sides".
549			if !c.publishReadyOrRetry(ctx, m, kind, ulid, subject, payload, elapsed, 0, true) {
550				return
551			}
552			c.metrics.recordSyncOutcome(ctx, provider, c.jurisdiction, outcomeNoop, elapsed)
553			_ = m.Ack()
554			if c.donePub != nil {
555				c.clearFailureIndex(ctx, kind, ulid, seq, viaRekick, true)
556			}
557		case dispositionTerm:
558			// Best-effort record, then Term regardless — fail open. recordTerminal
559			// logs + counts record_failed{cause} on a KV write failure; we Term
560			// either way rather than Nak, because the failure is permanent (re-running
561			// the sync would be wasted work) and a KV outage must not wedge the
562			// consumer. Recovery of a dropped record is owned by the record_failed
563			// alert + L2 reconcile, not by holding the message.
564			c.recordTerminal(ctx, kind, ulid, subject, payload, seq, failindex.ReasonPermanent, failindex.SourceWorkerPermanent, err)
565			slog.WarnContext(ctx, "Permanent sync error, terminating", slog.Any("error", err))
566			c.publishFailed(ctx, kind, ulid) // best-effort: tell entire-core the clone won't land
567			c.metrics.recordSyncOutcome(ctx, provider, c.jurisdiction, outcomeTerm, elapsed)
568			_ = m.Term()
569		case dispositionNak:
570			if isLastDelivery(m) {
571				// Final delivery: JetStream won't redeliver past consumerMaxDeliver,
572				// so this is terminal. Best-effort record (max_deliveries), then Term —
573				// fail open (recordTerminal surfaces a write failure via record_failed).
574				c.recordTerminal(ctx, kind, ulid, subject, payload, seq, failindex.ReasonMaxDeliveries, failindex.SourceWorkerExhausted, err)
575				slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "Sync failed; deliveries exhausted, terminating", slog.Any("error", err))
576				c.publishFailed(ctx, kind, ulid) // best-effort: clone exhausted retries, won't land
577				c.metrics.recordSyncOutcome(ctx, provider, c.jurisdiction, outcomeTerm, elapsed)
578				_ = m.Term()
579				return
580			}
581			slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "Sync failed", slog.Any("error", err))
582			c.metrics.recordSyncOutcome(ctx, provider, c.jurisdiction, outcomeNak, elapsed)
583			_ = m.NakWithDelay(consumerFailureDelay)
584		case dispositionRaced:
585			// Target ref moved between this job's plan and its push — a second sync
586			// of the same repo won the race (rapid webhooks, or a webhook
587			// overlapping the rekicker). Redeliver like a nak so the next delivery
588			// re-plans against the new tip and applies cleanly (usually a no-op,
589			// since the winner already mirrored the same source state), but record
590			// outcomeRaced + WARN so it stays out of the sync-failure alert's
591			// nak+term numerator: it self-heals and pages no one.
592			//
593			// Final-delivery escalation is identical to the nak path for the failure
594			// index + alert: if a repo somehow races every delivery to exhaustion the
595			// contention is no longer benign, so we record terminal (max_deliveries)
596			// and label outcome=term — that DOES reach the alert. Fail open on the
597			// index write exactly like dispositionNak.
598			//
599			// But we deliberately do NOT publish a 'failed' completion here. A raced
600			// error (ErrTargetRefMoved) means the target ref moved under us — i.e. a
601			// CONCURRENT sync of the same ULID is racing us, and one of those is the
602			// likely winner that publishes 'ready'. Emitting 'failed' would describe
603			// contention as an unclonable mirror; entire-core's MarkReady would heal
604			// it on the winner's event anyway, but skipping 'failed' avoids the
605			// misleading transient flip entirely. If no sibling ever wins (pathological
606			// — they can't all lose), status lingers at 'processing' and the failure
607			// index/alert still fire.
608			if isLastDelivery(m) {
609				c.recordTerminal(ctx, kind, ulid, subject, payload, seq, failindex.ReasonMaxDeliveries, failindex.SourceWorkerExhausted, err)
610				slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "Sync kept racing on target ref; deliveries exhausted, terminating", slog.Any("error", err))
611				c.metrics.recordSyncOutcome(ctx, provider, c.jurisdiction, outcomeTerm, elapsed)
612				_ = m.Term()
613				return
614			}
615			slog.WarnContext(ctx, "Sync raced on target ref; will retry", slog.Any("error", err))
616			c.metrics.recordSyncOutcome(ctx, provider, c.jurisdiction, outcomeRaced, elapsed)
617			_ = m.NakWithDelay(consumerFailureDelay)
618		}
619	}

621	// publishReadyOrRetry publishes the StatusReady completion and reports whether
622	// the caller may proceed to Ack. It returns true when the publish lands (or
623	// when no publisher is wired, or there's no ULID to key on) — the ack is safe.
624	//
625	// On a publish failure it does NOT ack: the completion is the only signal
626	// entire-core gets that the clone finished, and acking would drop it for good.
627	// Instead it Naks so JetStream redelivers before the final delivery. The
628	// next attempt re-runs the idempotent sync (a near-noop — refs already
629	// applied), and re-publishes. On the final delivery, retain the original
630	// message and capture the incomplete completion in the failure index for a
631	// re-kick. Never Ack or Term: even if KV is unavailable, the exhausted job
632	// remains inspectable/recoverable until stream retention expires. A successful
633	// sync is not a failed mirror: do not publish StatusFailed for this case.
634	func (c *consumer) publishReadyOrRetry(ctx context.Context, m ackableMsg, kind gitjobs.SourceKind, ulid, subject string, payload []byte, elapsed time.Duration, sourcePosition int64, noop bool) (proceed bool) {
635		if c.donePub == nil || ulid == "" {
636			return true
637		}
638		err := c.donePub.PublishCompletion(ctx, c.jurisdiction, c.clusterID, donejobs.Job{
639			RepoULID:       ulid,
640			Status:         donejobs.StatusReady,
641			SourcePosition: sourcePosition,
642			SourceKind:     string(kind),
643		})
644		if err == nil {
645			c.metrics.recordDonePublished(ctx, string(donejobs.StatusReady), true)
646			return true
647		}
648		c.metrics.recordDonePublished(ctx, string(donejobs.StatusReady), false)
649		if isLastDelivery(m) {
650			c.recordFailure(ctx, kind, ulid, subject, payload, streamSeq(m), failindex.ReasonMaxDeliveries, failindex.SourceWorkerCompletion, fmt.Errorf("sync succeeded but ready completion failed: %w", err), noop)
651			slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "Ready completion failed on final delivery; retaining job for recovery", slog.String("target_ulid", ulid), slog.Any("error", err))
652		}
653	
654		slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "Failed to publish mirror completion; naking to retry", slog.String("target_ulid", ulid), slog.Any("error", err))
655		c.metrics.recordSyncOutcome(ctx, string(kind), c.jurisdiction, outcomeNak, elapsed)
656		_ = m.NakWithDelay(consumerFailureDelay)
657		return false
658	}

660	// publishFailed publishes the StatusFailed completion on a best-effort basis:
661	// any error is logged and counted, never escalated. The message is already
662	// being Term'd (a permanent or retry-exhausted failure), so re-running the
663	// doomed sync to retry the publish would be wasted work; a lost 'failed' just
664	// leaves entire-core's row in 'processing' until the CLI's poll times out
665	// client-side — degraded, not incorrect. Mirrors the fail-open discipline
666	// recordTerminal already uses for the KV index.
667	func (c *consumer) publishFailed(ctx context.Context, kind gitjobs.SourceKind, ulid string) {
668		if c.donePub == nil || ulid == "" {
669			return
670		}
671		err := c.donePub.PublishCompletion(ctx, c.jurisdiction, c.clusterID, donejobs.Job{
672			RepoULID:   ulid,
673			Status:     donejobs.StatusFailed,
674			SourceKind: string(kind),
675		})
676		if err != nil {
677			slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "Failed to publish mirror failed-completion (best-effort, terminating anyway)",
678				slog.String("target_ulid", ulid), slog.Any("error", err))
679			c.metrics.recordDonePublished(ctx, string(donejobs.StatusFailed), false)
680			return
681		}
682		c.metrics.recordDonePublished(ctx, string(donejobs.StatusFailed), true)
683	}

685	// disposition is the JetStream action disposeResult takes for a sync result.
686	type disposition int
687	
688	const (
689		dispositionAck   disposition = iota // success → Ack
690		dispositionNoop                     // benign empty-source no-op → Ack
691		dispositionTerm                     // permanent failure → Term (no redelivery)

content.text:
Through a shared lock record in NATS. All `mirror-worker-github` pods in a cluster already share one NATS server, and its key-value store (JetStream KV) can do an atomic "create this key only if it doesn't exist" (`kv.Create`). The failure index (`mirror_sync_failed`) uses the same store today.

**How it works**

1. **Claim.** Before syncing, a worker calls `kv.Create("<target ULID>", {pod, stream seq, started_at})`. NATS guarantees only one caller can create a given key. The winner syncs. Everyone else gets `ErrKeyExists`, which means another worker is syncing this repo.
2. **Hold.** During the sync, the worker rewrites the key every 5 min, alongside the `InProgress()` ack extension it already sends. Each rewrite uses `kv.Update(key, value, lastRevision)`, so the write only succeeds if nobody else changed the key since the last read. The worker can tell if it has lost the lease.
3. **Release.** When the sync returns (success, failure or panic), the worker deletes the key, again only if it still holds it.
4. **Crash safety.** The bucket expires each entry after 15 min (`MaxAge`), the same as `AckWait`. If a pod dies mid-sync, its lease disappears about when JetStream redelivers its message, so nothing stays locked forever.

**Scope**
- The key is the target repo's ULID, so the lock is per repo, not per source.
- The eu-central-1 and us-east-2 placements are different targets with separate leases, so they still sync in parallel. That's correct: they write to different clusters.
- Within one region, Pod A would have held the lease, so Pod B and Pod C would have found the key and not started their own bootstraps. That's exactly the 22:47 and 22:48 duplicates.

**What a blocked job then does** is the open question I asked:
- **Mark the lease "dirty" and ack.** The holder sees the flag when it finishes and runs one more cheap sync.
- **NakWithDelay with growing delays.** Retry later and never record a failure while waiting.

I recommend dirty-and-ack. It never uses up `MaxDeliver`, and a burst of pushes during a long bootstrap collapses into a single follow-up sync. Which do you want?

You are a senior distributed-systems reviewer. Critically review a proposed design. Read-only: do not modify any files, push, or touch NATS. Read the code to ground your critique.

## Background (incident)
mirror-pipeline's `mirror-worker-github` pods consume git sync jobs from one JetStream durable per jurisdiction+cluster (`mirror-git-v1-<jurisdiction>-<cluster>`, stream `mirror_git_v1`, work-queue semantics, messages deleted on ack). Consumer config: AckExplicit, AckWait 15 min, MaxDeliver 10, no BackOff; a goroutine calls msg.InProgress() every 5 min (AckWait/3) while a sync runs; sync timeout 30 min. Publish dedup window is 1 s (MsgID per source+target). Jobs come from entire-core (on mirror creation) and `fanout` (one per GitHub push webhook, per placement); also rekicker, mirrorresume, native resync sweep.

On 2026-10-15 a new private 7 GB repo was bootstrapped (one-shot, ~3.5 min stream). Two GitHub pushes arrived mid-bootstrap; fanout published sync jobs; other pods picked them up, saw an empty target (a bootstrap writes no refs until it ends) and started 2nd and 3rd full bootstraps of the same target. Losers failed with `refs/heads/dev: already exists` (classified "raced" → NakWithDelay 30 s) but their 7 GB packs were already committed in entiredb (packs are committed before the ref update), leaving ~63 GB duplicates, and concurrent indexing spiked entiredb memory. Separately ~39k "raced" syncs in 15 days across ~740 repos (mostly small), leaving ~33k leaked small packs.

## Proposed design: per-target sync lease
- New JetStream KV bucket `mirror_sync_leases` (declared in fleet like `fleet/apps/nats-streams/base/kv-mirror-sync-failed.yaml`), bucket MaxAge 15 min (= AckWait).
- Key = target repo ULID. Before sync: `kv.Create(ulid, {pod, stream_seq, started_at})`; only one creator wins.
- Holder renews with `kv.Update(key, val, lastRevision)` on the existing 5-min InProgress extender tick; releases with a revision-guarded delete when sync returns (success/fail/panic).
- If the bucket can't be bound at startup, run without leases (fail-open), like the failure index.
- Different placements (eu vs us) are different target ULIDs → independent leases (intended).
- What a blocked job does — two candidates:
  A) "Dirty + ack": CAS-update the held lease to set dirty=true, then Ack the job. The holder, when its sync finishes, re-reads the lease; if dirty, it clears the flag and runs another (incremental) sync in-process before releasing (loop). Rationale: never burns MaxDeliver; N pushes during a long bootstrap collapse to one follow-up. If the holder dies, its own message is redelivered after AckWait and syncs latest state. If dirty-update CAS fails because the lease was released, retry acquire.
  B) NakWithDelay with escalating delay (1, 2, 4… min); on the final delivery while lease still held, Ack without recording a failure.
  The original write-up proposed plain NakWithDelay 30 s, which would exhaust MaxDeliver=10 in ~5 min during a 30-min-capped bootstrap and record false failures.

## Code to read
- /Users/nodo/work/tasks/investigation/mirror-pipeline/cmd/worker/consumer.go (handleGitJob, disposeResult, startInProgressExtender, dispositions incl. publishReadyOrRetry/completion publishing to entire-core, failure index clear/record)
- /Users/nodo/work/tasks/investigation/mirror-pipeline/cmd/worker/syncer.go (what a sync does; raced error classification in syncer_errors.go)
- /Users/nodo/work/tasks/investigation/mirror-pipeline/pkg/failindex/failindex.go (existing KV usage/CAS patterns)
- /Users/nodo/work/tasks/investigation/mirror-pipeline/pkg/gitjobs/jobs.go, cmd/fanout, cmd/rekicker (publishers), and docs/ for any existing ADRs about concurrency/ordering.
- Also check nats.go version in go.mod for KV features (per-key TTL needs server 2.11+; check fleet/apps/nats for server version).

## What I want
1. Is a KV lease the right mechanism at all, vs alternatives (e.g. per-target subject partitioning / consistent-hash routing so one consumer owns a target, JetStream `MaxAckPending`-style per-subject ordering, a stream with per-subject max msgs + discard new as a natural coalescer, writing a marker ref early in bootstrap, or entiredb-side protection)? Rank them.
2. Correctness holes in the lease: clock/TTL vs renewal timing, GC pauses / long stalls causing a lost lease while still syncing (split-brain), MaxAge semantics on KV updates, revision-guarded delete, NATS unavailability mid-sync, panic paths, shutdown/drain, interaction with completion publishing (ready/failed events to entire-core and mirror_repos.status), failure index, rekicker, the different source kinds (github, entiredb, entiredb-namespace) sharing one target ULID.
3. A vs B: which, and what breaks in each. For A specifically: lost-wakeup races (dirty set right as holder releases), holder that Terms or exhausts deliveries while dirty, what the blocked job's ack means for completion events and the failure index, unbounded re-sync loops under continuous pushes, the holder's sync timeout budget across loop iterations.
4. Anything simpler that gets 90% of the value.

Be concrete and skeptical; cite file:line. Give a clear recommendation and a short list of must-handle edge cases. Keep the report under 700 words.

The Fable reviewer agrees a per-repo lease is the right fix and recommends the "mark dirty" option. It found four real problems in how I'd planned it. I checked the two code claims behind them: the namespace scope (`syncer.go:125`, `:141-146`) and `failindex.RekickMsg`.

**The four problems and their fixes**

1. **The lease would expire too early.** A sync can run for up to 30 min, but I'd set the lease to expire after 15 min.
   - Ack extensions and lease renewals are sent separately and can fail independently, so a still-running bootstrap could lose its lease halfway. That would let a duplicate start, which is the incident again.
   - Fix: expire after ~40 min (sync timeout plus two renewals), renewed every 5 min.
2. **A dead holder could leave work that never runs.** If the holding pod dies, its job is redelivered, finds the dead pod's lease still there, and treats itself as blocked. Nothing ever syncs.
   - Fix: a job may take over the lease if the lease records its own stream sequence number, or if the lease is older than the sync timeout plus 2 min.
3. **One lease per repo would block unrelated syncs.** GitHub syncs and Entire-namespace syncs write different refs to the same target repo. If a namespace push is folded into a GitHub follow-up, it's lost, because GitHub syncs skip namespace refs.
   - Fix: key the lease by target ULID plus source kind.
4. **Re-syncing inside the finished job is fragile.** Running the follow-up in the same job shares the 30-min budget and a stale source-position snapshot, and continuous pushes could keep one pod busy forever.
   - Fix: the lease stores the latest blocked job. When the holder releases, it republishes that job as a fresh message (same pattern as `failindex.RekickMsg`). However many pushes arrive, they produce one follow-up job.

**Ordering and bookkeeping**
- A blocked job acks only after its "dirty" flag write has succeeded. The holder deletes the lease only if it is unchanged since it last read it with no dirty flag; otherwise it republishes first.
- The lease is released on every exit, including panics, shutdown and the case where publishing the ready event fails and the job is retried.
- A blocked job publishes no completion event and doesn't touch the failure index. It's counted under a new outcome, `deferred`, which stays out of failure alerts like `raced` does.
- Fleet needs the new KV bucket, publish permission on `$KV.mirror_sync_leases.>`, and a metric showing whether the bucket was bound.

**What the reviewer rejected**
- **Escalating NakWithDelay:** it still uses up deliveries and silently drops work on the last one.
- **Routing each repo to one worker:** it breaks KEDA autoscaling.
- **Collapsing duplicate jobs in the stream:** it drops follow-up pushes silently.
- **An early marker ref in git-sync:** git-sync would treat it as "resume", not "busy".

**Longer-term fix it suggests:** entiredb should refuse a second create-only push to an empty repo while one is already in flight. That protects against any client, not just mirror workers.

My take: the revised design is sound and still small. The lease also covers the ~39k smaller raced syncs, which should cut most of the leaked packs. ## Problem 1: the lease expiring while the sync is still running

**The problem.** I'd proposed a lease that expires after 15 min (`AckWait`), kept alive by renewing it on the 5-min ack-extension tick. Two facts break that:
- A sync is allowed to run up to 30 min (`defaultSyncTimeout`, `consumer.go:44`), longer than the lease.
- `msg.InProgress()` is a one-way publish with no reply (`nats.go@v1.52.0/js.go:3693`, sent with `sync=false`). A lease renewal is a separate request and can fail on its own. So "the ack deadline was extended" doesn't mean "the lease was renewed".

Example: a 25-min bootstrap with a couple of failed renewals loses its lease at minute 15. The next push's job then gets the lease and starts a second full bootstrap, which is the incident again.

**The fix: make the lease outlive the sync budget, so no renewal is needed.** The holder's sync is cancelled at 30 min (`context.WithTimeout`, `consumer.go:451`). If the lease's expiry (the bucket's `ttl` in fleet) is 45 min, it cannot expire while its holder is still within budget, whatever happens to NATS. Renewal then adds nothing, so I'd drop it, along with its failure modes and the "what if a renewal fails" handling.

**Lifecycle**
- **Claim:** `kv.Create(key, value)` before the sync. It works over a previous delete marker too; nats.go handles that (`kv.go:706`).
- **Release:** a delete after the result is handled, only if the lease still matches the version the holder created (`LastRevision`).
- **Holder dies:** the lease expires after 45 min at most. Problem 2 (taking over a dead holder's lease) shortens that.
- **Hung sync that ignores its context:** the lease still expires at 45 min. Renewal would have kept a dead lease alive forever, so this is better without it.

**Conditions it relies on**

| What could go wrong | What I'd do |
|---|---|
| `ENTIRE_WORKER_SYNC_TIMEOUT` is raised above the bucket TTL, or set to `0` (disabled) | At startup, compare `kv.Status().TTL()` with `syncTimeout + 10m`. If it's too short, log an error, set a "lease unbound" metric, and run without leases (fail-open), like the failure index. |
| The bucket TTL lives in fleet and the timeout in an env var, so they can drift apart | The startup check above catches it, and a comment in both places says to keep them in step. |
| Lease expiry uses the NATS server's clock | That's what we want: no worker clocks are involved. |

**Ruled out:** per-key TTL (`jetstream.KeyTTL`). The NATS server 2.14.4 we run supports it, but it would mean moving off the legacy KV API used everywhere in this repo. I also don't know whether NACK 0.34 can declare the `limitMarkerTTL` bucket setting it needs. A bucket-wide TTL does the same job.

**Fleet bucket:** `history: 1`, `ttl: 45m`, `replicas: 3`, small `maxBytes`, with no `preventDelete` needed because losing it only drops in-flight leases. I'd pair it with a publish permission on `$KV.mirror_sync_leases.>` for mirror-worker.

| NATS server | Yes, 2.14.4 (needs 2.11+) | `fleet/apps/nats/base/helmrelease.yaml:37` |

- If `syncTimeout = 0` (disabled), the worker falls back to a fixed maximum such as 2h and logs a warning.
- When a lease expires instead of being released, the server leaves a marker (that's what `limitMarkerTtl` enables). An expiry means the holder crashed or hung, so we can count those markers as a metric.

**The catch: only `Create` attaches a TTL**

- Both upcoming fixes update the lease:

Every write to this bucket goes through the helper, so no version is ever stored without a TTL. A dirty-flag update resets the lease to a full TTL; problem 2's takeover rule limits how long that can keep a dead lease alive.
2. **Never update the lease key.** Takeover becomes a guarded delete followed by `Create`, and the dirty flag lives under a separate key. That's more keys and more races to reason about, and the separate key still needs the helper to get a TTL.
3. **Fall back to the bucket-wide TTL** for anything written without a per-key TTL. Simple, but it brings back the fleet-versus-worker coupling we're trying to remove.

## Problem 2: a dead holder's lease

**The problem.** A pod can die mid-sync: OOM, eviction, node loss or SIGKILL. Its lease stays in KV until it expires, up to 45 min. Meanwhile:

1. The dead pod's message stops getting ack extensions. JetStream redelivers it within 15–20 min, since extensions were every 5 min and `AckWait` is 15 min.
2. That redelivery lands on another pod and finds the lease held by the dead pod.
3. The blocked-job rule marks the lease dirty and acks the job. **The original sync job is now gone.**
4. Any push jobs in that window are marked dirty and acked too.
5. The lease later expires and the dirty flag disappears with it. Nobody republishes, so nothing ever syncs.

For a new mirror, `mirror_repos.status` stays at `processing` until the next push happens to arrive, which may be never.

There's a second trap: each dirty update rewrites the lease and restarts its 45-min clock. So pushes arriving after the holder died keep its lease alive longer.

**The fix: two takeover rules.** The lease value records `{pod, stream_seq, kind, started_at, dirty}`, and `started_at` is kept unchanged on dirty updates. A job that finds the lease held checks these, in order:

| Rule | Condition | Why it's safe |
|---|---|---|
| **Own sequence** | `lease.stream_seq == my stream seq` | This is the holder's own job, redelivered. JetStream only redelivers when the holder stopped extending the ack for 15 min, so the holder is dead or cut off from NATS. This catches a crash in 15–20 min instead of 45. |
| **Age** | `now − lease.started_at > syncTimeout + 2m` | Any holder that is still alive has had its sync cancelled by then. This covers what the first rule misses, for example a holder that acked its message but died before releasing the lease. |

**Taking over** is `kv.Update(key, newValue, lease.revision)` with this pod's details, a fresh `started_at`, and `dirty` cleared.
- Clearing `dirty` is correct because the new holder's sync starts after every push that set it, so it picks those pushes up.
- If two jobs try to take over at once, the revision check lets one win. The other re-reads the lease, finds a live holder, and becomes a normal blocked job.

**If the old holder was alive after all.** Rule 1 can fire on a holder whose ack extensions failed for 15 min while its sync kept running, for example if it lost NATS but could still reach GitHub. Then:
- Two syncs run at once, which is what happens today in that case, so it's no worse.
- When the old holder finishes, its revision-checked delete fails because the revision changed. It concludes it lost the lease and does nothing: no delete and no republish. The new holder handles any dirty work.

**What's still not covered:** if a holder finishes and acks, but every attempt to release the lease fails, a dirty flag set during its sync has no one left to act on it. Rule 2 only fires when another job arrives. To shrink that window, release retries 3× with backoff and counts a `lease_release_failed` metric. If it still fails, that push is only picked up by the next push. I'd accept that: it needs a NATS outage at exactly that moment.

If the old holder keeps going after a takeover, its result still lands on the shared message. That could set off a chain of takeovers, so the design needs one more rule: **a holder that has lost its lease steps aside.**

**Why its result still counts.** JetStream tracks an outstanding message by its stream sequence, not by which delivery it went to. In nats-server 2.14.4:
- An ack or term from a stale delivery is accepted: it's looked up in `o.pending[sseq]` regardless of delivery number (`consumer.go:3695`).
- A NAK is accepted if the message is still pending (`consumer.go:3164`).
- `InProgress` extends the message for whoever currently holds it (`consumer.go:2810`).

So once P2 has taken over, P1's acks, NAKs and extensions all still affect the same message.

**What happens without a fix**

| P1 (old holder) ends with | Effect | Bad? |
|---|---|---|
| Success, then Ack | Message removed. P2's later Ack or NAK does nothing. | No: the repo is synced. |
| Failure, then NAK | The message is redelivered 30 s later to P3. P3 sees `stream_seq == its own`, so the own-sequence rule fires and P3 takes over from P2, which is still running. That's a third concurrent sync, and it can keep going. | **Yes** |
| Permanent error, then Term with a `failed` event | entire-core marks the mirror failed while P2 may still succeed. P2's `ready` later fixes it, but the status flips back and forth. | Yes |
| Exhausted retries | P1 writes a failure-index entry that may be false. | Yes |

**Fix: a holder that lost its lease steps aside**
- **Before disposing of its result,** the holder reads its lease with `kv.Get`. If the lease now belongs to someone else, it doesn't ack, NAK or term the message, publishes no completion event, and writes nothing to the failure index. It only logs and counts `lease_lost`. The new holder owns the outcome.
- **Stop early:** on each 5-min extender tick, the holder also does a `kv.Get`. If the lease clearly belongs to someone else, it cancels its sync. Cancelling mid-push aborts entiredb's receive before the pack is committed, so the duplicate 7 GB pack never lands.
- **Only act on proof:** if the `Get` itself fails, which is likely in the cut-off-from-NATS case that triggered the takeover, the holder carries on. It only steps aside when it can see the lease belongs to someone else.

**What's left:** a tiny race window. P1 checks and still owns the lease, P2 takes over, then P1 NAKs. That needs a takeover to land in the milliseconds between P1's check and its NAK. At worst it causes one extra sync, not an endless chain.

This brings back a periodic `Get` on the extender tick, but it's read-only. Nothing renews the lease, so problem 1's "the lease can't expire while its holder is within budget" still holds.

A worker can be wrongly declared dead, and then two workers hold the same job. The fix is that the one who lost the lock quietly gives up and leaves the outcome to the other.

**The situation.** Think of the lease as a "this repo is being worked on" sign on a door.
1. Worker A takes the job and hangs the sign with its name on it.
2. A loses contact with NATS for a while but keeps working. To NATS, A looks dead.
3. NATS hands the same job to Worker B. B sees A's sign, decides A is dead, and swaps in its own name.
4. Now A and B are both doing the same job, and only B's name is on the door.

**Why that's a problem.** A doesn't know it was replaced, so when it finishes it reports on the job as if it still owned it. NATS doesn't care who reports: any report on that job counts.
- **A succeeded:** fine, the job is done.
- **A failed and says "retry later":** NATS hands the job to Worker C. C sees B's sign, decides B must be dead too, and takes over. Now three workers are on the same repo, and it can keep growing.
- **A hit a permanent error:** A tells entire-core "this mirror failed" while B may still succeed, so the status flips back and forth.

**The fix.** Before A reports anything, it looks at the door. If the sign no longer has its name, A stays silent: no "done", no "retry", no "failed". B finishes the job and reports for both.

A also checks the door every 5 minutes while working. If its name is gone, it stops right away, before uploading a duplicate 7 GB copy.

If A can't reach NATS to read the sign, it keeps working. It only gives up when it can actually see someone else's name.

## Problem 3: what the lease key covers

**What I found: two source kinds write to the same repo.** A GitHub mirror placement gets two kinds of sync jobs:

| Kind | Source | Refs it writes | Worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| `github` | GitHub | Everything except `refs/heads/entire/native/*` (`syncer.go:125`) | `github` durable |
| `entiredb_ns` | The Entire home repo | Only `refs/heads/entire/native/*` (`syncer.go:141-146`) | Its own `native-ns` durable (`roles.go:38`) |

Native mirrors (kind `entiredb`) are separate target repos, so they never share a ULID with a GitHub mirror.

**The reviewer's concern, with a lease keyed by ULID only:**
- A namespace job blocked behind a GitHub sync marks the lease dirty and is acked.
- On release, the holder republishes the stored job. If the dirty flag only stores one job, a GitHub push and a namespace push overwrite each other, and one is lost.
- The reviewer's fix is to key by ULID plus kind, so the two kinds run independently. Their ref sets don't overlap, so they never race on a ref.

**Where I disagree: refs don't overlap, but data does.** The native branches branch off the same history as `main`.
- If a namespace sync runs while the GitHub bootstrap is still filling an empty target, the target has nothing to compare against. The namespace sync sends its branches' entire history: another multi-GB pack, indexed at the same time.
- That recreates the incident with a different second writer.
- entiredb doesn't care which refs a push targets. The thing to protect is "one large ingest per repo at a time".

**My proposal:** one lease per target ULID, with a pending slot per kind.

```
lease key   = <target ULID>
lease value = { pod, stream_seq, kind, started_at,
                pending: { "github": <subject+payload>,
                           "entiredb_ns": <subject+payload> } }
```

- **Any job, any kind:** if the lease is held, the job writes its own subject and payload into `pending[its kind]`, checked against the lease's revision, then acks.
- **On release:** the holder republishes each pending entry to its own subject, so a namespace job goes back to the namespace durable. Then it deletes the lease, again checked against the revision. The worker already has publish rights on `mirror.>`.
- **Several pushes of the same kind** collapse into one entry, and the latest wins. That's safe because a sync always reads the source's current state, not the push's contents.
- **Takeover (problem 2):** the new holder clears only the pending entry for its own kind. Its sync covers that kind but not the other one.

**Costs**
- A namespace sync can wait up to one GitHub sync, at most 30 min during a bootstrap. In steady state, GitHub syncs take seconds.
- The lease value gets a little bigger, holding two payloads at most.

**Open question:** I haven't checked whether git-sync also uses refs outside the namespace scope as "already have these" hints. If it doesn't, namespace syncs send more data than needed even in steady state. That's a separate inefficiency to verify, and it would only strengthen the case for one lease.

Do you agree with one lease per target and a pending slot per kind, rather than the reviewer's per-kind key? Then problem 4: republishing on release instead of re-syncing in place.

## Problem 4: what happens to deferred jobs

**What changed since the review:** problem 3 rules out re-syncing in place. A pending namespace job may need a different worker role (`native-ns`, with no GitHub token) than the GitHub holder. So the holder can't run it itself; it has to put it back on the queue. The reviewer's other reasons for avoiding an in-process loop still apply:
- it would share the holder's 30-min budget and its pre-fetch source-position snapshot (`consumer.go:398`),
- it would tie up one pod indefinitely under continuous pushes.

### The blocked job
1. It tries `kv.Create` and finds the key exists.
2. It runs problem 2's takeover checks. If neither applies, it continues.
3. It writes itself into `pending[kind]` = `{subject, payload, stream_seq, rekick, traceparent}`, using `kv.Update` checked against the revision it just read.
   - If the revision changed, it goes back to step 1. That covers the holder releasing at the same moment, which is how this design avoids losing a wake-up.
4. It acks only after that write has succeeded.

What the blocked job deliberately doesn't do:
- **No completion event:** it didn't sync. The republished job will report.
- **No failure-index write:** it neither failed nor succeeded.
- **New outcome `deferred`:** counted in a metric and kept out of failure alerts, like `raced`.

Two details get carried through to the republished job:
- `rekick` keeps the `Mirror-Rekick` header, so a rekicked job still clears its failure-index entry as `via=rekick`.
- `traceparent` links the republished job's trace back to the push that caused it.

### Holder release, on every outcome while the holder still owns the lease
1. Read the lease. If it isn't ours, step aside (problem 2).
2. For each `pending` entry not yet republished in this release:
   - publish it to its stored subject with a fresh `Nats-Msg-Id`, using the same contract as `failindex.RekickMsg`,
   - remember its `stream_seq` locally, so it isn't sent twice.
3. Delete the lease, checked against the revision from step 1.
   - If the revision changed, someone added a pending entry while we published, so go back to step 1. The local set means only the new entry gets published.

**Ordering:** release runs before the holder's own Ack, NAK or Term. That makes a failed republish recoverable:

| Republish fails after 3 retries, and the holder's outcome was | Then |
|---|---|
| Success (would Ack) | Switch to a delayed NAK and keep the lease. The redelivery takes over through problem 2's own-sequence rule. Its sync is cheap, because the refs were just applied, and it retries the republish when it releases. |
| Transient failure (NAK) | Already coming back. Keep the lease, and the next delivery handles it. |
| Permanent failure (Term) | Keep the lease, which still holds the pending entries. They're republished when the next job for this repo takes over, or lost when the lease expires after 45 min. Accepted: it needs a permanent error and a NATS failure at the same moment. |

### Properties
- **Coalescing:** however many pushes arrive during a sync, at most one follow-up job per kind is published.
- **Bounded:** each republish is a new message with its own budget and delivery count. Under continuous pushes, the rate is one follow-up per sync cycle.
- **Duplicate-free:** checking the revision on delete, plus the local republished set, means an entry is published once per release.

### Small additions
- The lease value holds up to 2 job payloads, a few hundred bytes each.
- The `mirror-worker` NATS user already publishes to `mirror.>`. Problem 1's fleet change adds `$KV.mirror_sync_leases.>`.

Do you agree with deferred jobs coming back as fresh messages, with release ordered before the holder's own Ack, NAK or Term? That covers all four problems. Next I can write the design up, or start implementing, starting with the git-sync size-check fix.

# Providers park refused pack stages and admit them once confirmed

Date: 2026-10-15
Status: Accepted
Amends: [`20261009-provider-history-gate.md`](20261009-provider-history-gate.md)
Relates to: `docs/runbooks/history-gate-refusals.md`

## Context

The history gate refuses a write whose parent is missing on the provider. The
gate ADR expected a repair to fill the gap in minutes. That holds when writes
are rare.

On 2026-10-15 a mirror pushed to one repo every 7 to 60 seconds during a
rolling deploy. Three restarted providers fell behind. Each refused push was
the parent of the next push, so each next push was refused too. A repair fetch
takes a snapshot of the refs when it starts. It ends behind the writes that
arrive during the transfer. The providers caught up only when the pushes
stopped, 1 h 45 min later. Meanwhile each repo had two working replicas.

Faster repair fetches (trail 4127) shrink the window, but they cannot close it:
a fetch that takes longer than the gap between writes still ends behind.

A repair that fetches again until the refs stop moving was rejected. Each round
carries only the pushes of the last one, but it ends only when a fetch is faster
than the gap between writes. On 2026-10-15 the gaps were 7 to 60 seconds and an
incremental fetch took about 10, so the loop could run for the whole burst.
Parking converges after one fetch, whatever the write rate.

## Decision

A provider keeps a pack stage that its gate refused, and admits the stage once
the push is confirmed and the provider holds the stage's parents.

1. **Park.** On a gate refusal, the provider records the stage in memory: its
   pack hash, its stream trailer, and its staged time. The staged files stay
   on disk, as they do today.
2. **Confirm.** After a push commits with quorum, the coordinator sends
   `ConfirmPack` to each provider whose gate refused the stage. A stage is
   admitted only after this confirm, so a provider never makes canonical a
   pack whose push failed fsck, connectivity or quorum.
3. **Admit.** After a repair transfer, a catchup fetch or heal, the boot
   drain, and each confirm, the provider checks its confirmed stages, oldest
   first. A stage whose parents are all
   present commits like a push: it is promoted, or ingested as loose objects.
   An admitted stage can hold the parent of a later one, so the pass repeats
   until it admits nothing.

A stage resolves the bases of a thin pack from local storage, and from the
repo's other providers when the node lacks a base. A lagging node usually
lacks the bases of the first push after its restart. Without the fallback,
that stage fails before the gate runs, so it is never parked, and every
later thin push fails the same way. The coordinator waits for every provider
stage, so the fallback is bounded: 256 peer reads and 10 seconds per stage.
Past that, the stage fails at once, as before.

Each repo has at most one admission pass. A confirm or a repair that arrives
during a pass makes the pass go again.

`ConfirmPack` names the push by the end of the pack stream, up to 32 bytes.
Every provider receives the same stream. A thin-pack rebuild gives each
provider its own pack hash, so the hash cannot name the push.

### Bounds

- A stage is admissible for `ParkedPackMaxAge`, 30 minutes from its staged
  mtime. Admission is a stage-to-commit path, so it stays inside
  `PackfileIngestDeadline`. The quarantine sweep reclaims staged files only
  after 45 minutes, so admission never races it.
- An unconfirmed or expired entry is forgotten. The sweep deletes its files.

# One mirror sync per target at a time, through a KV lease

Date: 2026-10-16
Status: Proposed
Relates to: [`20260521-mirror-bootstrap-on-create.md`](20260521-mirror-bootstrap-on-create.md), mirror-pipeline `docs/design/mirror-sync-failure-index.md`

## Context

Mirror workers pull sync jobs from one durable per placement and kind. Nothing
stops two workers from syncing the same target at once. The 1 s publish dedup
window only collapses retries of one publish.

On 2026-10-15 a new private 7 GB GitHub mirror took about 3.5 minutes to
bootstrap. Two GitHub pushes arrived during that time. Fanout published a job
for each. Other workers saw an empty target, because a one-shot bootstrap
writes no ref until it ends, and started two more full bootstraps. Each loser
failed on `refs/heads/dev: already exists` after its pack was committed. That
left about 63 GB of duplicate packs, and concurrent indexing took nodes to
61 of 61.9 GB.

The same race happens on small repos all the time: 39k raced syncs and 33k
leaked packs in the 15 days to 2026-10-15.

## Decision

A worker holds a lease on the target repo while it syncs. A job that finds the
lease held leaves a note in it and acks. The holder republishes the notes as
fresh jobs when it finishes.

### Lease

- KV bucket `mirror_sync_leases`, declared in fleet: `history: 1`, `ttl: 45m`,
  `limitMarkerTtl` set so expiries are visible.
- Key: target repo ULID. Value:
  `{pod, stream_seq, kind, started_at, pending: {<kind>: job}}`.
- Acquire with `kv.Create`. Nothing renews the lease: its 45 min TTL outlives
  the 30 min sync budget, so it cannot expire under a live holder.
- At startup the worker checks that the bucket TTL is at least the sync
  timeout plus 10 min. If not, or if the bucket is missing, it syncs without
  leases and reports it on a metric, like the failure index.

One lease covers every kind that writes the target. A GitHub sync and an
`entiredb_ns` sync touch different refs, but on an empty target either one
sends the full shared history.

### Blocked job

1. `kv.Create` fails because the key exists.
2. Takeover check (below). If it applies, take over and sync.
3. Otherwise write itself into `pending[kind]` with `kv.Update` at the read
   revision, replacing any older note of that kind. On a revision conflict,
   go back to step 1.
4. Ack. Record outcome `deferred`: no completion event, no failure-index
   write, excluded from failure alerts like `raced`.

A note keeps the subject, payload, stream sequence, rekick header and trace
context, so the republished job behaves like the original.

### Release

The holder runs this before its own Ack, Nak or Term:

1. Read the lease. If it is no longer ours, step aside (below).
2. Republish each pending note to its subject with a fresh `Nats-Msg-Id`, as
   `failindex.RekickMsg` does. Skip notes already republished in this release.
3. Delete the lease at the read revision. On a conflict, go back to step 1.

If republishing still fails after 3 retries, keep the lease. A successful sync
then Naks instead of acking, so the redelivery takes over and retries the
release.

### Dead holders

A blocked job takes over the lease with `kv.Update` at the read revision when:

- `lease.stream_seq` equals its own stream sequence. JetStream redelivered the
  holder's job, so the holder stopped extending it for 15 minutes; or
- `now - started_at` is more than the sync timeout plus 2 minutes.

The new holder clears the pending note of its own kind; its sync covers it.

### Stepping aside

A holder that finds its lease taken does not Ack, Nak or Term, publishes no
completion, and writes nothing to the failure index. Otherwise its Nak would
redeliver the job, the redelivery would match the own-sequence rule, and a
third sync would start. JetStream accepts acks and naks from any delivery of a
message.

The holder reads its lease on each 5 min extender tick and cancels its sync
when the lease is clearly someone else's. If it cannot read the lease, it keeps
going.

## Consequences

- One sync per target. Pushes during a sync collapse into one follow-up per
  kind.
- A namespace sync can wait up to one GitHub sync: 30 minutes at most during a
  bootstrap, seconds otherwise.
- The race packs stop accumulating. Existing leaked packs still need a full
  repack.
- One more KV bucket, and the worker needs publish permission on
  `$KV.mirror_sync_leases.>`.
- Remaining gap: if every release attempt fails after a Term, its notes wait
  for the next job on that repo or are lost when the lease expires.

## Alternatives considered

- **Nak with delay while the lease is held.** Every Nak counts toward
  `MaxDeliver = 10`. A 30 minute bootstrap exhausts it, and the waiting job is
  recorded as a failure.
- **Re-sync in the holder.** It shares one sync budget, keeps one pod busy
  under continuous pushes, and cannot run another kind's sync.
- **Per-key TTL.** `kv.Update` drops the TTL, so a takeover or a note would
  make the lease permanent. Every write would need a custom publish.
- **Lease per target and kind.** It lets a namespace sync push the full
  history next to a GitHub bootstrap.
- **Route each target to one consumer.** It breaks KEDA scaling per durable.
- **Per-subject limits in the stream.** They drop the follow-up push without
  any signal.
- **Refuse a second create-only push in entiredb.** Worth doing for any
  client, but not instead of this: the mirror still wastes the transfer.

## Related fix

git-sync chooses batched bootstrap from the GitHub repo size, but asks the API
without credentials. For a private repo the call returns 404 and git-sync
falls back to one pack without logging. git-sync will authenticate the call
and log the outcome. That fix is separate from this ADR.

## Open questions

- Does a namespace-scoped sync use refs outside its scope as haves? If not, it
  sends more history than needed even in steady state.

input.title: git-sync: authenticate the GitHub repo-size preflight and log its outcome
input.description:
git-sync picks batched bootstrap (512 MiB packs) when the GitHub API reports a repo over 1.5 GiB. The size lookup sends no credentials, so for a private repo GitHub returns 404. git-sync then falls back to a one-shot bootstrap without logging anything. Private repos of any size therefore bootstrap as one pack.

On 2026-10-15 this sent the private 7 GB repo `energio-es/main` as one 7 GB pack. Combined with concurrent bootstraps (COR-2166), it pushed prod entiredb nodes to 61 of 61.9 GB of Go memory.

## Cause

- `internal/strategy/bootstrap/bootstrap.go:1849-1882` (`lookupGitHubRepoSizeKB`) calls `httpConn.HTTP.Do(req)` and never applies `httpConn.Auth`. Auth only goes on git smart-HTTP requests (`internal/gitproto/smarthttp.go:218-222`).
- Every non-200 response, transport error or parse error returns `0, false` silently (`:1867-1881`). `githubBatchLimit` (`:1828-1847`) then keeps the one-shot path.
- The "selected batched mode" message goes through `p.log`, which needs `Verbose`. mirror-worker doesn't set it, so the decision never reaches Datadog.
- Same code in every git-sync version since v0.5.0, including `main` (`013012ac`), which mirror-pipeline pins.
- Public repos are also at risk: unauthenticated calls share GitHub's 60 requests/hour per egress IP.

## Fix

- [ ] Apply `gitproto.ApplyAuth(req, httpConn.Auth)` before `Do` in `lookupGitHubRepoSizeKB`. The installation token as basic auth (`x-access-token`) is accepted by the REST API.
- [ ] Log the preflight outcome (HTTP status or error, size in KB, chosen mode) through `PushLogger`/`BootstrapLogger`, which mirror-worker already wires without verbose mode.
- [ ] Tests: private repo (404 without auth, 200 with auth → batched), lookup failure → one-shot with a logged warning.
- [ ] Bump git-sync in mirror-pipeline.
